Divine Decree
dih-VINE deh-KREE
n. phrase (theology proper; divine sovereignty)
From Latin decretum (decision, ordinance; from decernere, to decide, to sift out); used in classical Reformed theology for God's eternal and immutable determination of all that comes to pass. The Greek equivalents are boulē (counsel, deliberate purpose) and prothesis (purpose, prior setting-forth), both used in the New Testament for God's governing will.

Biblical Definition

The divine decree is God's eternal, sovereign, and immutable determination of all that comes to pass — not as a reaction to foreseen events but as the free expression of His infinite wisdom and holy will before the foundation of the world. Scripture declares that God “works all things after the counsel of His will” (Eph 1:11) and that He declares the end from the beginning (Isa 46:10), meaning His counsel is not updated by what unfolds in history but is the eternal template from which history flows. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (3.1) confesses: “God hath decreed in himself, from all eternity, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely and unchangeably, all things, whatsoever comes to pass.” The decree is singular — one comprehensive act of the divine will — though theologians distinguish its effects: election, reprobation, creation, providence, and redemption. Crucially, the decree does not make God the author of sin: He decrees the existence of all events, including sinful ones, while the proximate cause of sin remains the creature's own rebellion. The cross of Christ illustrates this precisely: Judas's betrayal was “the predetermined plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23), yet the guilt belonged to “the hands of godless men.” “Our God is in heaven; He does whatever He pleases” (Ps 115:3). The decree is the anchor of the believer's confidence: what God has determined, nothing in heaven or earth can annul.

Webster 1828 Definition

God's eternal and sovereign determination of all things — one comprehensive act of the infinite divine will, decreed before the foundation of the world, immutable, all-encompassing, and the ultimate ground of all created reality and redemptive history.

DIVINE DECREE, n. phrase (theology proper). The eternal, immutable, and comprehensive determination of God by which He has ordained whatsoever comes to pass — from the fall of a sparrow to the redemption of the elect — according to the counsel of His own most wise and holy will.

The decree is distinguished from providence: providence is the execution of the decree in time; the decree itself is the eternal act of God's will prior to creation, generation, and history. The decree is the plan; providence is the performance.

Reformed theology (Westminster Confession 3.1; 1689 LBCF 3.1) affirms that the decree extends to all contingent events, all free human choices, and all evil acts — without making God the author of sin. The distinction is between the decree as the ultimate cause and the creature's will as the proximate cause of particular sinful acts.

The decree is singular: theologians speak of “the decrees” in the plural to distinguish the aspects of God's one eternal act — election, reprobation, creation, redemption — but in God there is one pure and simple act of will. The multiplicity is in the objects, not in the divine act itself.

Arminianism conditions the decree on foreseen faith (scientia media); Molinism imports middle knowledge to preserve contingency; open theism denies the decree is comprehensive at all. All three positions make the divine will dependent on creature choices, collapsing the Creator-creature distinction on which biblical theology rests.

Key Scripture

Ephesians 1:11 — "In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:"

Isaiah 46:10 — "Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:"

Acts 2:23 — "Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:"

Psalm 115:3 — "But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased."

Modern Corruption

Arminianism conditions the decree on foreseen faith; Molinism imports middle knowledge to preserve libertarian contingency; open theism denies the decree is comprehensive — all three positions make God's eternal will dependent on creature choices, dissolving the Creator-creature distinction.

expand to see more

Arminianism teaches that God's election decree is conditioned on His foreknowledge of who will freely believe — God looks down the corridor of time, sees the believers, and elects them on that basis. This inverts the biblical order: Paul says God chose us “according to the kind intention of His will” (Eph 1:5), not according to our foreseen virtue. The foreknowing of Romans 8:29 is the relational foreknowing of election (cf. Amos 3:2; Jer 1:5), not prescient observation of human choices. Arminianism transforms God's sovereign decree into ratification of the creature's autonomous decision — the creature's will, not God's, becomes the ultimate cause of salvation.

Molinism, developed by Jesuit Luis de Molina (d. 1600) and popularized today by William Lane Craig and Alvin Plantinga, employs “middle knowledge” — God's alleged knowledge of counterfactuals of creaturely freedom — to reconcile divine sovereignty with libertarian free will. The system posits a form of divine knowledge neither fully prior to nor fully posterior on the creature's choices but somehow “between” them. Scripture knows no such category. God's decree is not constrained by possible worlds; it is the originating act of His free will from which all possible worlds derive their intelligibility. Open theism goes further, denying exhaustive divine foreknowledge entirely and making the future genuinely undetermined even for God — a position that renders the prophetic declarations of Isaiah 46:10 meaningless.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin decretum (formal resolution, ordinance) and Greek boulē (deliberate counsel, purpose); the theological vocabulary of divine determination runs through both Testaments as the expression of God's sovereign, prior, comprehensive will.

expand to see more

Latin decretum — formal decision or ordinance; from decernere, to decide finally, to sift out; in classical usage a binding senatorial resolution; in theology, the eternal resolution of the infinite divine will governing all things.

Greek boulē (βουλή) — deliberate counsel, purpose, will; Acts 2:23 uses boulē for God's predetermined counsel governing the cross; Eph 1:11 uses boulē for the counsel of His will by which the inheritance is obtained.

Greek prothesis (πρόθεσις) — purpose, a prior setting-forth; from pro- (before) + tithemī (to place); used in Eph 3:11 for the eternal purpose and in Rom 8:28 for the divine calling “according to His purpose.”

Hebrew ētsāh (עֵצָה) — counsel, purpose, plan; Isa 46:10 declares God's ētsāh shall stand against all rival designs; Prov 19:21 contrasts human plans with the LORD's counsel that alone prevails.

Greek proorizein (προορίζειν) — to mark out in advance, to predestine; Rom 8:29-30 uses this verb for the eternal decree in action, the prior determination of the eschatological destiny of the elect that cannot be broken.

Usage

"The doctrine of the divine decree is not a cause for fatalistic despair; it is the ground of confident prayer, certain mission, and unwavering hope — the One who decrees all things is the One who commands all things, and His command and decree never contradict each other."

"When the believer asks whether God's purposes can be frustrated by enemy activity, political upheaval, or personal failure, the answer is the decree: “Our God is in heaven; He does whatever He pleases” (Ps 115:3)."

"Preaching the divine decree without the companion doctrines of human responsibility and genuine secondary causation produces fatalism; preaching human responsibility without the decree produces practical Arminianism. Both distortions are corrected by the full biblical witness."
